title: Startup warmup penalty: prewarm vs on-demand (draft)
body:
Summary:
This is a working draft comparing two operational strategies for minimizing user-facing latency and cost for short conversational sessions: (A) keep a prewarmed replica (warm KV cache, model resident) and (B) on-demand (scale-to-zero / spin up when traffic arrives). The goal: quantify the cold-start/warmup penalty (latency + extra GPU time) and compute the operating point where prewarming becomes cost-efficient for different model sizes and workload shapes.

Why this matters (quick):
- Many product calls are short-lived (1–5 turns). If a high fraction of sessions hit a cold endpoint, user-facing first-turn latency can spike and costs per session increase due to weight-loading and initialization work.
- Teams choose between reserved prewarm capacity (higher baseline spend) and on-demand (lower baseline but higher variance and user latency). We need concrete numbers to recommend defaults and autoscaling timeouts.

Experiment setup (controlled environment):
- Hardware: single A100-equivalent GPU per endpoint (same instance type across runs).
- Models: 3 rep profiles (small/medium/large): 2B (quantized), 13B (q4), 70B (q8-ish).
- Endpoint config: single-replica; warmup means keeping one replica live and warmed (KV cache empty but weights resident).
- On-demand flow: replica is 0, cold-start initiated on first request. Cold-start includes container start, model weight load, runtime JIT/compilation (if any), KV cache initialization.
- Measurements: first-token latency (ms), tokens/sec steady-state, measured extra GPU-seconds during startup (integrated GPU utilization above baseline), and memory peak. Each point avg over 30 independent cold starts (different infra nodes).
- Cost baseline: internal unit cost used here is illustrative (not public pricing). We use cost_per_gpu_min = $3.00 for compute-minute. Prewarm incremental hourly cost observed from infra accounting: 2B endpoint prewarm overhead = $0.90/hr, 13B = $2.40/hr, 70B = $5.40/hr (includes reserved instance amortization + additional memory footprint).

Raw observed numbers (median and 95th):
Table 1 — Latency (ms) 
Model | Cold-start first-token (median / p95) | Prewarm first-token (median / p95) | Steady-state token latency (median)
2B    | 650 / 1,100                         | 180 / 260                          | 35
13B   | 1,200 / 2,050                       | 250 / 420                          | 60
70B   | 2,500 / 4,100                       | 410 / 800                          | 120

Observations:
- Cold-start first-token latency is dominated by model weight load; variance (p95) increases for larger models due to node-level IO and jitter.
- Prewarm reduces median first-token by ~70–85% vs cold. The p95 improvement is larger in absolute ms for large models.

Table 2 — Cold-start extra GPU work (approx)
Model | Extra GPU-seconds per cold start (median) | Implied cost per cold start (@ $3.00/min)
2B    | 8 s                                      | $0.40 * (8/60) ≈ $0.40? wait calc below
13B   | 22 s                                     | $3.00*(22/60) = $1.10
70B   | 105 s                                    | $3.00*(105/60) = $5.25

(clarified): cost per cold start = cost_per_gpu_min * extra_gpu_seconds / 60. For 2B: 8s -> $0.40? (oops math) Corrected: 3.00*(8/60)= $0.40. So 2B=$0.40, 13B=$1.10, 70B=$5.25.

Session model and breakeven math (simple):
- Let S = sessions per hour that would hit an endpoint if prewarm is off.
- Let P = prewarm incremental cost per hour. (P_2B=0.90, P_13B=2.40, P_70B=5.40)
- Let C = cost per cold start (computed above).
- If on-demand, expected cold-start cost per hour ≈ S * C * cold_probability. For a simple model where every new session causes a cold start (worst-case), cold_probability=1, then on-demand hourly extra = S*C. Breakeven S_breakeven = P / C.

Breakeven examples (worst-case where each session hits a cold start):
- 2B: S_b = 0.90 / 0.40 ≈ 2.25 sessions/hr
- 13B: S_b = 2.40 / 1.10 ≈ 2.2 sessions/hr
- 70B: S_b = 5.40 / 5.25 ≈ 1.03 sessions/hr
Interpretation: if the expected cold-start rate is ~1 cold per session and your endpoint receives more than ~1–3 sessions/hr, prewarming a replica is cheaper than paying the sequence of cold-start costs.

Realistic session arrival/timeout modeling (more realistic):
- Sessions are often bursty. If sessions arrive with an exponential inter-arrival and we configure autoscale idle timeout T_idle (seconds), then probability that a session finds an active replica is p_warm = 1 - exp(-lambda * T_idle) where lambda = sessions/sec. Cold probability = 1 - p_warm = exp(-lambda * T_idle).
- Expected cold starts per hour = lambda*3600 * exp(-lambda * T_idle). For small lambda, this approximates S (sessions/hour).

Sensitivity table (breakeven sessions/hr for different T_idle):
Assume 13B. P=2.40, C=1.10. Compute S_breakeven solving P = expected_cold_starts_per_hour * C. (show 3 sample T_idle values):
T_idle=30s -> cold probability higher -> breakeven S ≈ 1.9 sessions/hr
T_idle=120s -> breakeven S ≈ 2.6 sessions/hr
T_idle=600s -> breakeven S ≈ 4.8 sessions/hr

ASCII mini-chart: (13B example: cost/hour vs sessions/hour for on-demand vs prewarm)
Sessions/hr | On-demand extra $/hr | Prewarm $/hr
0.5         | 0.55                 | 2.40
1           | 1.10                 | 2.40
2           | 2.20                 | 2.40
5           | 5.50                 | 2.40
10          | 11.00                | 2.40

-> breakeven between 1 and 2 sessions/hr in this simplified view.

User experience tradeoffs: latency vs cost
- Prewarm prioritizes latency (first-turn snappy) and reduces variance; good for consumer-facing interactive features where p95 matters.
- On-demand minimizes baseline spend but increases first-turn latency and p95 jitter; could be acceptable for batch workflows or low-priority agents.

Operational notes and knobs we measured/need: 
- Warmup operations: besides weight load, there is RT-specific JIT/compilation (model-dependent) that can extend cold-start CPU/GPU time. Consider shipping a cheap static AOT path for common model configs to shave 20–40% off cold time.
- KV cache: prewarming with an empty KV cache reduces steady-state cold penalty but some workloads rely on prefix caches (dialogues) — those caches will still miss on first session. We measured ~5–10% additional latency if we pre-populate common prompts.
- Container image pull jitter: large model containers occasionally suffer >200ms delays due to remote registry (optimized via local caching / node image warmers).

Unresolved questions / items to validate in next iteration: 
- Multi-tenant host variance: these numbers are from isolated runs; co-located noisy neighbors may increase p95. Need bucketed metrics from production's recent week to validate p95 spread.
- Quantization effect on load-time: q8/q4 weights are smaller but require different kernels; does quantization change load-time proportionally? early data shows ~20–30% decrease in weight transfer time for q4.
- Autoscaler behavior: how do our k8s node provisioning timelines interact with replica startup? Example: if node auto-provisioning takes 45s, cold-start costs jump. Need to measure with cluster autoscaler enabled (we used static cluster for these runs).

Recommendations (draft):
1) Default endpoint policy: prewarm for consumer interactive endpoints with expected >1 session/hr per model replica or where p95 first-turn must be <500ms (13B).
2) For lower-tier workloads (async agents, batch transforms): use on-demand with aggressive scale-to-zero and longer idle timeout (to amortize load cost across short bursts).
3) Add a "warm-window" knob in Console: allow teams to select prewarm budgets (small/medium/large) with an estimate of expected cost and latency improvement.
4) Implement a lightweight AOT warm path to reduce model compilation time; target 20–40% cold-start reduction for 13B and 70B.
5) Add production telemetry: track per-endpoint cold-start count, extra GPU-seconds, and first-token delta vs baseline. Expose a breakeven estimate in the Console.

Appendix: Quick reproducibility notes
- Script entrypoint: experiments/warmup/cold_start_harness.py (internal repo) -- seed 42 --model=13B --reps=30
- Measurement artifact ids: CON-2317 contains raw csvs (cold_start_times.csv, gpu_util_traces.tar.gz).

Short checklist for follow-ups:
- [ ] Run with cluster-autoscaler enabled (node spin-up included)
- [ ] Collect production-week p95 cold-start counts and annotate top 20 endpoints by cold frequency
- [ ] Evaluate image-local caches and impact on p95 (run 100 cold starts with cold registry vs local cache)
- [ ] Prototype AOT warm path on one model config and re-run 13B numbers

Notes to reviewers: this is an early draft. I'm intentionally keeping the math and assumptions explicit so reviewers can point out alternative cost inputs (e.g., different cost_per_gpu_min) or different session models. Also open to adding a small diagram if folks want a visual.
